topComments.author: irdc
topComments.text: This is why system programming still matters. topComments.author: strenholme
topComments.text: With my own MaraDNS, I aggressively optimized the memory usage of blacklist entries by having a single really big malloc() to allocate the memory for the entries, then traversing that memory block for potentially blacklisted entries. When I was using one malloc() per entry, a large blacklist took up 237 megabytes of memory. The same blacklist, once optimized to be loaded with a single malloc() call, only took up 9.5 megabytes of memory. https://samboy.github.io/blog/entries/MaraDNS.html#BlogEntry...

topComments.author: OptionOfT
topComments.text: > we store the records as a single Box<[u8]> containing each record encoded as a 2-byte length prefix followed by its raw bytes. Interestingly this is exactly how netlink works-ish: https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/focal/man3/netlink.3.ht... You start, get the type & length, and then that is how many bytes you read. Some issues with that when you deserialize, from a raw stream in to `[u8; 4096]` buffer, the alignment is only guaranteed to be on 1 byte, not 4 bytes. In practice it is 4 bytes, but if you run those tests with Miri, you'll get yelled at. So the fix there is to declare the buffer with a type that mandates the alignment of the largest type that you're going to be deserializing. So then you start your buffer as follows: `[u32; 1024]`, and with `slice::from_raw_parts` you get to turn that into `[u8; 4096]` with the expected alignment. As an exercise I wrote a streaming parser for netlink, the current existing package serializes everything, all at once.

stories.summary: Cloudflare optimized its 1.1.1.1 DNS cache system to reduce memory usage by 100 terabytes through engineering improvements. The article details the technical optimizations made to their DNS infrastructure to achieve this significant efficiency gain. Read this if you're interested in how large-scale DNS systems can be optimized and the engineering decisions behind managing massive caching operations.

stories.title: Doctors are finally learning to manage antidepressant withdrawal
stories.author: eutropheon

topComments.author: classichasclass
topComments.text: Though this article concentrates on the SSRIs, other meds like the SNRIs can have a similar or even worse withdrawal effect. We didn't call it "Side Effexor" for nothing. People legitimately need these drugs, including in the short term. The problem for acute stressors once they resolve is how to get them back off.

topComments.author: D-Machine
topComments.text: Best way to manage the withdrawal would be to dramatically reduce them being prescribed in the first place. The linked article says they have "small to moderate effectiveness", but this is being far too generous. The correct way to measure drug effectiveness is if the treatment meets the standard of a minimal important difference. I.e. you measure depression on various rating scales, like the 17-point HAM-D, and research suggests a minimal important difference (i.e. one patients and clinicians can actually notice) needs to be about 3-5 points. But the average effects of almost all antidepressants do not meet these thresholds, i.e. the effect actually appears practically invisible. [1] Then you'll get waffling like "oh, but it really has a big effect for some people", but, well, no, we've looked at that too, and the placebo groups get just as miraculous "big effects", i.e. evidence supporting the idea "they really help some people" is also largely lacking [2-3]. All the other attempted saves ("oh, but eventually you find one that works for you") are also not really well supported either [4]. Like, maybe they really help some people, but it is far, far less clear than most assume, and should be balanced with concerns like withdrawal and serious side effects like emotional blunting and sexual dysfunction. EDIT: And just to be clear to anyone doing a drive-by downvote thinking this is about recent asinine US politics, it emphatically isn't. There are serious methodological concerns here that desperately need to be communicated to the public. [1] https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593736/ [2] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7451660/ [3] https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33175895/ [4] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11844611/

It got me through a rough patch, and seems (in combination with therapy, and some life changes) to have rewired me a little. Symptoms I had for a decade prior have not returned. And I’m not sure I could have made those life changes without it. Sadly my arachnophobia came back though. Oh well.

stories.summary: Medical professionals are increasingly recognizing that withdrawal symptoms from long-term SSRI use are more common and severe than previously understood, prompting major health organizations to develop better guidelines for safely discontinuing these widely-prescribed medications. The article explores how SSRIs became dominant treatments due to their safety profile compared to earlier antidepressants, but this perceived safety led to inadequate monitoring and minimal guidance on dose reduction, leaving many patients on these drugs long-term without proper withdrawal management protocols.

stories.summary: This article presents an efficient O(n) algorithm for computing the volume of a 3D triangulated mesh by applying the divergence theorem to reduce a triple integral to a simple per-triangle calculation. The method requires only 11n floating-point operations total, making it fast enough to process millions of triangles per frame on modest hardware. The author derives a compact formula that computes volume by summing contributions from each triangle's vertices and their cross product.

stories.summary: Small modular reactors (SMRs) are emerging as a promising solution to nuclear power's challenges, offering cheaper and faster construction than conventional reactors by using factory-built components assembled on-site. stories.summary: Rising bot activity in email inboxes—from 2% to 16% in consumer emails since 2023—is contaminating click metrics that advertisers rely on, with Gmail seeing particularly sharp increases in bot clicks. Publishers and email platforms are responding by introducing "verified clicks" that filter out automated interactions, allowing them to charge advertisers a premium for guaranteed human engagement. This shift could reshape how digital advertising is measured and priced in the email industry.

stories.title: Show HN: Talos – An AI agent with a permission kernel between model and shell
stories.author: kurdman_007

topComments.author: kurdman_007
topComments.text: Hi HN — maker here. I built Talos because I wanted to hand an agent a terminal without handing it my trust model. Every tool call (read, write, exec, delegate) passes a small deterministic kernel, ~645 lines of Python, that returns allow, needs-human or deny. Unattended runs can't ask, so needs-human becomes deny. The agent can never grant itself anything. Around that kernel: 23 gated tools, a UID-separated worker for delegated code, MCP servers confined to that worker from an operator-owned registry (no marketplace, no third-party code in the agent process), a hash-chained audit log, Ed25519-signed updates verified before anything unpacks, and a read-only live dashboard that has no approve button, by design. Numbers the CI enforces on every page of the site: 2063 tests, 179/179 adversarial cases, 645 kernel lines, 0 inbound ports. The site has a browser reimplementation of the policy kernel you can poke at without installing anything, a replayed real session, and an honest comparison to OpenClaw and Hermes — including what Talos doesn't have (breadth; that's doctrine, not backlog). Happy to answer anything — especially the parts where the design is wrong. Site: https://talos-agent.ch — Source (MIT): https://github.com/talos-kernel/talos

stories.summary: Talos is an AI agent that runs Claude in a sandboxed environment with a deterministic security kernel that individually authorizes each tool call before execution, preventing unauthorized file access, secret exposure, and system damage. The system uses a "permission first" design philosophy with multiple safety layers—protected paths, sandboxing, reversibility checks, and human approval gates—rather than trying to add security after the model's capabilities are built. It's designed to be strong enough to give real shell access to while remaining verifiable and controllable, with 179 adversarial test cases validating its security decisions.

stories.title: ALMA Reveals Long-Lived Hotspots on Betelgeuse's Bubbling Surface
stories.author: layer8
stories.summary: ALMA observations of the red supergiant star Betelgeuse reveal an uneven surface with persistent hotspots that are surprisingly stable—remaining in nearly the same location for at least seven years, longer than current models predict. The hotspots, caused by enormous convective motions and shocks in the star's atmosphere, are up to 800 K hotter than surrounding gas and vary the star's apparent radius by about six percent. These high-resolution observations provide unprecedented insights into Betelgeuse's structure before it eventually explodes as a supernova.

stories.summary: Moniepoint's Cloud Engineering team proactively rebuilt their Kafka infrastructure from manual VM management to Strimzi (Kafka on Kubernetes) before experiencing a crisis, recognizing that their ad-hoc setup didn't scale despite functioning. The shift to Strimzi with Kubernetes operators eliminated manual SSH operations, standardized deployments through YAML templates, and provided namespace isolation and unified fleet management. This case study illustrates how systems thinking involves identifying architectural problems early and making deliberate improvements before they become disasters, rather than only reacting to incidents.

stories.title: Terry Rozier and the Teleprompt Operator
stories.author: surprisetalk
stories.summary:
# Summary

NBA player Terry Rozier was indicted in 2025 for tipping off associates about leaving a game early so they could place over $200,000 in profitable bets on his underperformance—a scheme made possible by the massive growth of legal sports gambling from $4.8 billion (2017) to $160+ billion (2025). The article argues that while legalization does enable better detection of fraud, it simultaneously creates the market liquidity necessary for large-scale insider betting schemes that would have been impractical in illegal markets. The author illustrates this double-edged sword by contrasting Rozier's case with a more recent incident involving a White House teleprompter operator betting on prediction markets—demonstrating how legalization doesn't just police vice better, but fundamentally expands opportunities for corruption.
